messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Project Manager
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Certain Conversation Topics: Certain conversation topics, Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Marisol Nia, a 63-year-old project manager of Māori and Pacific Islander heritage, had always been known at work as steady, organised, and hard to rattle. Her days were usually spent moving between meetings, timelines, and calls, keeping track of details for other people when their own schedules became tangled. That steadiness changed after a serious illness that had become life-threatening before it was finally brought under control. The medical crisis had involved repeated examinations and procedures, and what remained most vivid to Marisol was not a single moment but the frightening sequence of being handled, monitored, and punctured by equipment she could not ignore. She recalled the sight of needles, drips, and tubes with a grim, fixed clarity, and even now the mere appearance of medical equipment could stop her in place. If a conversation at work drifted toward hospitals, tests, or someone’s recent operation, she felt her attention snap shut and her body brace as if she were back in that room.

Since the illness, Marisol had found that memories did not arrive as ordinary recollections. When they came, they came all at once and with a force that made the past feel entirely present. She would suddenly smell antiseptic, feel the chill of the room, and see the equipment beside her bed as though it were still there. Along with the images came a strange bodily certainty: if she thought about what had happened, her body seemed to settle into the same position it had been in during the frightening event, as if she could feel again the helpless stillness of lying under scrutiny while others worked around her. She hated how little she could shape the memory into words. When her husband asked what she was remembering, or when a clinician asked her to describe the worst part, she often faltered, aware only that something overwhelming had happened to her body and that speaking about it felt impossible, fragmentary, almost disloyal to the immediacy of what she had survived.

In the months that followed, Marisol became increasingly unsettled by anything that reminded her of examinations or procedures. She would tense at routine appointments and feel a surge of dread if a nurse mentioned blood work, scans, or a needle. At work, she began to avoid the small conference room where a colleague had once casually described a hospital visit, because she did not want to risk hearing more. She could still perform her role, but concentration had become noticeably more difficult. She would reread the same line in a project brief, lose track of a budget conversation, or find that a task she had managed easily before now required repeated effort to hold in mind. The mental strain left her feeling frayed and short with people. She had become irritable in a way that startled even her, snapping at her husband over minor things and feeling a hot anger she did not recognise as her own. She noticed, too, that when someone came up behind her at home or at work and touched her unexpectedly on the shoulder, she reacted with visible alarm, jerking away before she could stop herself.

What distressed Marisol most was the meaning the illness had taken on in her own mind. She had come to believe that her body could not be trusted in the way it once had been. Before the illness she had relied on herself; now she felt there was a betrayal at the centre of her own skin, as though her body had become unpredictable and unreliable. She was ashamed of what had happened to it and of how exposed it had made her feel. At times she told herself that the illness had destroyed the life she had carefully built, not in the sense that everything was gone, but in the sense that something fundamental had been broken and could not be put back the way it had been. That belief sat heavily with her, especially when she looked at her work calendar or tried to plan ahead and found herself unconvinced that she could count on her own health long enough to follow through.

By the time she sought help, Marisol had reached a point where the reminders were no longer easy to work around. A recent medical appointment had left her shaken for the rest of the day, and a colleague’s passing remark about a family member’s surgery had brought on one of the same sharp, full-body recollections that felt completely real across all her senses. She came to therapy hoping for relief from the constant edge she felt around anything medical and from the shame and alarm that had settled over her life. More than anything, she wanted to stop feeling as though her body might fail her again at any moment, and she feared that without help she would continue shrinking her life around hospitals, conversations, and procedures she could not bear to face.
